title: Balanced equations for burning alkanes
keyIdea: When an alkane burns completely in plenty of oxygen, every carbon atom ends up in carbon dioxide and every hydrogen atom ends up in water. Balance the equation in order: carbon first (n carbons make n CO₂), hydrogen next (2n + 2 hydrogens make n + 1 H₂O), oxygen last (count the O atoms in the products and halve to get O₂). For alkanes with an even number of carbons the O₂ comes out as a half, so double every coefficient: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O. The general rule is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + (3n + 1)/2 O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O, so each extra carbon needs 1½ more O₂.
familyTip: Pick an alkane from the gas cooker or a camping stove (methane, propane, butane) and balance it together on the back of an envelope: carbons first, then hydrogens, then oxygens. Ask your teenager to predict, before working it out, which one needs a doubled equation, and why.

visual.caption: Does the alkane balance with whole numbers straight away, or does it need doubling? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: step coefficients and watch a C, H and O atom ledger; balance propane, double a half O₂ for butane, and slide n to find the rule.

kid: When an alkane burns in plenty of air, it reacts with oxygen. All its carbon ends up in carbon dioxide, and all its hydrogen ends up in water. Atoms are not made or lost, so a balanced equation has the same number of each atom on both sides.

Balance in a set order. Carbon first: propane, C₃H₈, has 3 carbons, so it makes 3CO₂. Hydrogen next: 8 hydrogens make 4H₂O, because each water has 2. Oxygen last: the right side now has 3 × 2 + 4 = 10 oxygen atoms. Each O₂ brings 2, so you need 5O₂.
Leave oxygen to the end because it turns up in both products. Change only the big numbers in front. Never change the small numbers inside a formula, because that makes a different substance.

Butane, C₄H₁₀, makes 4CO₂ and 5H₂O. That is 13 oxygen atoms, which is 6½ O₂. You cannot round to 7, so double everything instead: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O. Each extra carbon adds one CO₂ and one H₂O, which needs 1½ more O₂.
adult: Ages 14 to 16. GCSE chemistry (AQA 4.7.1.3, OCR and Edexcel equivalents) expects students to write balanced symbol equations for the complete combustion of alkanes. The products are carbon dioxide and water. The general formula of an alkane is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so the general equation is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + (3n + 1)/2 O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O.

Work in a fixed order. Balance carbon first, since it is only in CO₂. Balance hydrogen next, since it is only in H₂O. Balance oxygen last, since it is in both products and comes from just one reactant. When n is even, 3n + 1 is odd, so the O₂ needed is a half. Doubling every coefficient gives whole numbers, for example 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O and 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. Some mark schemes accept the half; whole numbers are always safe.

Common mistakes: changing subscripts (writing C₃H₈O₂) instead of coefficients; writing one H₂O per hydrogen atom; counting oxygen atoms but forgetting to halve for O₂; rounding 6½ up to 7, which breaks the balance; and doubling the reactants but not the products. Be careful too with state symbols if asked: water is often shown as a gas, H₂O(g), at flame temperature.

In the lab your teenager steps the coefficients up and down while an atom ledger compares C, H and O on each side. They balance propane in the C, H, O order, then butane with O₂ moving in halves and a 'double everything' button. Last, they slide the chain length from methane to octane to find which alkane needs 8, 9½ and 12½ O₂, which reveals the 1½ O₂ per carbon rule.

practice.prompt: Which equation for the complete combustion of propane is balanced?
practice.hint: Count O on the right: 2 in each CO₂ and 1 in each H₂O.
practice.explain: 3 × 2 + 4 = 10 O atoms on the right, so 5O₂ on the left. 8H₂O would hold 16 H, but propane has only 8.

practice.prompt: An alkane has {n} carbon atoms. How many molecules of water form when one molecule burns completely?
practice.hint: The formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Each H₂O holds 2 hydrogens.
practice.explain: It has 2 × {n} + 2 hydrogens, and 2 go into each water, so {=n+1} H₂O.

practice.prompt: Two molecules of an alkane with {n} carbons burn completely. How many O₂ molecules are needed?
practice.hint: Two molecules make 2n CO₂ and 2(n + 1) H₂O. Count O, then halve.

practice.prompt: Balancing butane gives C₄H₁₀ + 6½O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O. What is the whole-number equation?
practice.hint: Multiply every coefficient by the same number.
practice.explain: Doubling every coefficient keeps the balance. Rounding to 7O₂ gives 14 O on the left but 13 on the right.

practice.prompt: One molecule of an alkane with {n} carbons burns completely. How many oxygen atoms are in the products?
practice.hint: Add the O in {n} CO₂ to the O in the water molecules.
practice.explain: {n} CO₂ hold 2 × {n} O and {n} + 1 H₂O hold {n} + 1 O, which is {=3*n+1} O atoms.

pool.prompt: What are the products of the complete combustion of an alkane?
pool.explain: With plenty of oxygen, carbon becomes CO₂ and hydrogen becomes H₂O. Carbon monoxide forms when oxygen is short.

pool.prompt: In which order should you balance an alkane combustion equation?
pool.hint: Leave the element that is in both products until last.
pool.explain: C is only in CO₂ and H only in H₂O, so fix them first. O is in both products, so it goes last.

pool.prompt: Which equation for ethane is balanced with whole numbers?
pool.hint: One ethane makes 2CO₂ and 3H₂O, which hold 7 O atoms.
pool.explain: 7 O atoms need 3½ O₂, so double everything: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O.

pool.prompt: A student balances propane as C₃H₈O₂ + ... What went wrong?
choices: They changed a formula instead of a coefficient
pool.hint: Small numbers inside a formula say what the substance is.
pool.explain: Adding O₂ to the formula makes a different substance. Only change the big numbers in front.

pool.prompt: An alkane with {n} carbons burns completely. How many CO₂ molecules form from one molecule?
pool.hint: Each carbon atom ends up in its own CO₂.
pool.explain: One CO₂ for each carbon, so {n} carbons make {n} CO₂.

pool.prompt: Why does octane need more oxygen per molecule than methane?
choices: It has more C and H atoms to turn into CO₂ and H₂O
It burns at a higher temperature
Its molecules are heavier, so they fall slower
pool.hint: Count the atoms that need oxygen.
pool.explain: C₈H₁₈ makes 8CO₂ and 9H₂O, which hold 25 O atoms. CH₄ makes CO₂ and 2H₂O, which hold 4.

pool.prompt: Which alkanes give a half O₂ in a one-molecule equation?
choices: Those with an even number of carbons
Those with an odd number of carbons
pool.hint: O₂ needed is (3n + 1) ÷ 2. When is 3n + 1 odd?
pool.explain: If n is even, 3n is even and 3n + 1 is odd, so halving leaves a half. Ethane, butane and octane need doubling.

pool.prompt: An alkane has {n} carbons. How many hydrogen atoms does one molecule have?
How many O₂ are needed to burn one molecule of pentane, C₅H₁₂?
pool.hint: Make 5CO₂ and 6H₂O, count the O atoms, then halve.
pool.explain: 5 × 2 + 6 = 16 O atoms, which is 8O₂. 16 is the atom count, not the number of O₂.

pool.prompt: In a doubled equation, 2 molecules of an alkane with {n} carbons burn completely. How many CO₂ molecules form?
pool.hint: Each molecule makes one CO₂ per carbon, and there are two molecules.
